newsitem.title: JAPAN: Ex-Nomura executives' homes raided as probe widens.
newsitem.headline: Ex-Nomura executives' homes raided as probe widens.

text.p: Prosecutors Friday raided the homes of former Nomura Securities executives and racketeers behind a payoff scandal at the country's biggest brokerage.
As the investigation widened, speculation grew about whether the probe would uncover more examples of preferential treatment for important Nomura clients, possibly including politicians.
Japanese media said the company had about 10,000 VIP accounts whose owners received special treatment.
Company officials said the account owners received no undue benefits in shares traded for them and just got the preferential service due large clients.
In the latest humiliation for the company, prosecutors raided the homes of former Nomura Chairman Setsuya Tabuchi and former President Yoshihisa Tabuchi, who is unrelated.

They also searched the homes of "sokaiya" racketeers Ryuichi Koike and his younger brother, who were arrested Thursday on suspicion of taking 50 million yen ($431,000) in payments from Nomura after threatening to disrupt the company's 1995 annual meeting.
Japanese securities law bans brokerages from making payments to racketeers who extort money from companies by threatening to disrupt shareholder meetings with awkward questions.

Prosecutors say the elder Koike was the brains behind the scheme while his younger brother's real estate firm was used as a front to receive the money. The payments to the company are also believed to have violated another law that bars brokers from reimbursing clients for investment losses, by funnelling profits earned elsewhere into the account.
Earlier this week, two other former Nomura executives and a manager in charge of Nomura's shareholder meetings were arrested in the scandal.
It was the second time the two Tabuchis were in hot water.
They resigned in 1991 after similar revelations that the top brokerage firm compensated elite clients for losses and that affiliates dealt with organised crime.
But the two rejoined Nomura's board in 1995, despite being associated with the firm's old reputation for aggressively grabbing profits at the expense of small investors' interests.
Since the scandal broke in March after an internal probe, Nomura's president and 15 board members also resigned.
At the heart of the investigation is whether the firm's executive board was aware of the payoffs to Koike or whether the officials involved acted on their own.
Government officals are presenting the investigation as a warning to financial markets as a whole that the era of lax enforcement of regulations is over.
Shoichi Royama, a key member of a panel working on reforms of the securities industry, said that the Nomura case had highlighted the need for reform.

"The scandal has given Japanese society and the securities industry itself the impression that reform of the securities industry is needed," said Shoichi Royama, a member of the Securities and Exchange Council and a professor at Osaka University.
"We would like to establish a market in Japan which is sound, even if there are some troublesome brokers," he told reporters.
The Asahi Shimbun said Koike had boasted to friends that he regularly wined and dined Nomura executives.
It said sources close to Koike had said he often told his friends that he was so close to some Nomura people that they called him "aniki" -- an affectionate term for an elder brother.
The scandal has already cost Nomura, a firm at the financial heart of Japan since the 19th century, some of its biggest clients.
